title: Chapter 34 — The Cabin-Table
paragraphs: It is noon, and Dough-Boy, the steward, thrusts his pale bread-dough face from the cabin hatch to announce dinner to his lord and master. Ahab, sitting in the lee quarter-boat, has just been taking a reading of the sun and is now silently calculating the latitude on the smooth, medallion-shaped tablet set into the upper part of his ivory leg for this daily purpose. From his complete inattention to the news, you'd think moody Ahab hadn't heard his servant. But presently, catching hold of the mizzen shrouds, he swings himself to the deck and, in an even, unenthusiastic voice, says, "Dinner, Mr. Starbuck," and disappears into the cabin.

When the last echo of his sultan's step has faded and Starbuck, the first Emir, has every reason to believe he is seated, then Starbuck rouses from his stillness, takes a few turns along the deck, and after a serious glance into the compass, says with some touch of pleasantness, "Dinner, Mr. Stubb," and goes below. The second Emir lounges about the rigging a while, then slightly shakes the main brace to make sure it's secure. He likewise takes up the old refrain and, with a quick "Dinner, Mr. Flask," follows his predecessors.

But the third Emir, now finding himself alone on the quarter-deck, seems relieved of some curious restraint. Tipping all sorts of knowing winks in every direction and kicking off his shoes, he breaks into a sharp but silent hornpipe right over the Grand Turk's head below. Then, by a clever trick, he tosses his cap up to the mizzentop for a shelf, and goes down rollicking — at least as far as he's visible from the deck — reversing all other processions by bringing up the rear with music. But before stepping into the cabin doorway, he pauses, puts on a completely new face, and then the lively, independent little Flask enters King Ahab's presence in the role of the humble slave.

It is not the least of the strange things bred by the artificial customs of the sea that, while on the open deck some officers will speak boldly and defiantly to their commander, those same officers, the very next moment going down to dinner in that commander's cabin, will show an inoffensive, almost apologetic and humble manner toward him as he sits at the head of the table. This is remarkable, and sometimes quite comical. Why the difference? A puzzle? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon, and to have been Belshazzar not arrogantly but graciously — in that there must have been some touch of worldly grandeur. But the man who presides in a truly royal and intelligent spirit over his own dinner table of invited guests exercises an unchallenged power and personal influence that transcends even Belshazzar's, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Anyone who has once dined with friends has tasted what it is to be Caesar. There is a social spell in it that no one can resist. Now, if you add to this the official authority of a ship's captain, you can work out the cause of that peculiarity of sea life just described.

Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on a white coral beach, surrounded by his fierce but still respectful cubs. Each officer waited to be served in his proper turn. They were like small children before Ahab. And yet in Ahab there seemed to lurk not the slightest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened on the old man's knife as he carved the main dish. I don't think that for anything in the world they would have broken that moment with the slightest remark, even on a topic as neutral as the weather. No! And when Ahab, reaching out his knife and fork — the slice of beef locked between them — motioned Starbuck's plate toward him, the mate received his meat as though receiving charity, and cut it tenderly, and flinched a little if the knife happened to scrape the plate, and chewed it silently, and swallowed it carefully. For like the Coronation banquet at Frankfurt, where the German Emperor formally dines with the seven Imperial Electors, these cabin meals were somehow solemn events, eaten in terrible silence. And yet old Ahab never actually forbade conversation — he himself simply said nothing. What a relief it was to stifled Stubb when a rat made a sudden racket in the hold below. And poor little Flask — he was the youngest son, the little boy of this grim family party. His were the shinbones of the salt beef — his would have been the drumsticks. For Flask to have presumed to serve himself would have felt like committing theft. If he had helped himself at that table, he probably could never have held his head up again in honest company. Nevertheless, strange to say, Ahab never actually forbade him. And had Flask helped himself, chances are Ahab would never have so much as noticed. Least of all did Flask presume to help himself to butter. Whether he thought the ship's owners denied it to him on account of its clouding his clear, sunny complexion, or whether he believed that on so long a voyage in such remote waters butter was a luxury not meant for a subordinate — however it was, Flask, alas, was a butterless man!

Another thing: Flask was the last person down to dinner and the first one back up. Consider! This meant Flask's dinner was badly squeezed for time. Starbuck and Stubb both got a head start on him, yet they also had the privilege of lingering. If even Stubb, who ranks only one peg above Flask, happened to have a small appetite and showed signs of finishing his meal, then Flask had to hurry — he wouldn't get more than three mouthfuls that day, for it was against sacred custom for Stubb to leave the table before Flask. Therefore Flask once confided in private that ever since he had risen to the dignity of an officer, he had never known what it was to be anything other than hungry, more or less. What he ate didn't so much relieve his hunger as keep it alive forever. Peace and satisfaction, Flask thought, have departed from my stomach for good. I am an officer — but how I wish I could grab a bit of good old-fashioned beef in the forecastle, the way I used to as a common sailor. There's the fruit of promotion. There's the vanity of glory. There's the insanity of life! Besides, if any ordinary sailor on the Pequod had a grudge against Flask in his official capacity, all that sailor had to do for ample revenge was go aft at dinnertime and peek at Flask through the cabin skylight, sitting there tongue-tied and dumbfounded before the awesome Ahab.

Now, Ahab and his three mates formed what might be called the first table in the Pequod's cabin. After their departure, in reverse order of their arrival, the tablecloth was cleared — or rather restored to some hasty order by the pale steward. Then the three harpooners were invited to eat, being the leftover heirs of the feast. They made a sort of temporary servants' hall of the grand cabin.

In sharp contrast to the barely tolerable restraint and nameless invisible domination of the captain's table was the complete carefree liberty of the harpooners. While their masters, the mates, seemed afraid of the sound of their own jaws, the harpooners chewed their food with such gusto that you could hear it. They dined like lords. They filled their bellies like cargo ships being loaded with spices. Such tremendous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego that to fill the gaps left by the previous meal, poor pale Dough-Boy often had to bring out a huge slab of salt beef that looked as if it had been quarried from a solid ox. And if he wasn't quick about it, Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of hurrying him along by throwing a fork at his back, harpoon-style. And once Daggoo, seized by a sudden whim, helped Dough-Boy's memory by snatching him up bodily and shoving his head into a big empty wooden platter, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began tracing the circle on his scalp preliminary to scalping him. He was naturally a very nervous, trembling sort of little fellow, this bread-faced steward — the offspring of a bankrupt baker and a hospital nurse. And what with the constant terrifying spectacle of the dark Ahab and the periodic tumultuous visits of these three savages, Dough-Boy's whole life was one continuous quivering lip. Usually, after providing the harpooners with everything they demanded, he would escape into his little pantry next door and fearfully peek out at them through the slats of the door until it was all over.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated facing Tashtego, filing his teeth against the Indian's. Across from them, Daggoo sat on the floor, since a bench would have brought his plumed head up against the low ceiling beams. With every motion of his enormous limbs, the low cabin framework shook, as when an African elephant rides as a passenger in a ship. But for all that, the great man was wonderfully restrained, even dainty, in his eating. It seemed hardly possible that such comparatively small bites could fuel the vitality spread through so broad, lordly, and magnificent a person. But doubtless this noble savage fed deeply on the abundant element of air, breathing in the sublime life of the worlds through his wide nostrils. Not by beef or bread are giants made or nourished. But Queequeg had a savage, barbaric smacking of the lips while eating — an ugly sound — so much so that the trembling Dough-Boy almost checked his own lean arms for teeth marks. And when he heard Tashtego call for him to come out so his bones could be picked, the simple-witted steward nearly shattered all the crockery around him in the pantry with sudden fits of terror. Nor did the whetstones the harpooners carried in their pockets for their lances — and with which, at dinner, they would pointedly sharpen their knives — do anything to calm poor Dough-Boy. How could he forget that in his island days, Queequeg must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, cannibalistic indiscretions? Alas, Dough-Boy! Hard life for the white waiter who serves cannibals. He should carry not a napkin on his arm but a shield. In good time, though, to his great relief, the three sea-warriors would rise and depart — to his credulous, story-hungry ears, their martial bones jingling at every step, like Moorish swords in scabbards.

But though these harpooners dined in the cabin and officially lived there, being anything but sedentary in their habits, they were hardly ever in it except at mealtimes and just before bedtime, when they passed through it to their own quarters.

In this one matter, Ahab was no different from most American whale captains, who generally believe that by rights the ship's cabin belongs to them and that anyone else is allowed in only as a courtesy. So in truth, the mates and harpooners of the Pequod could more properly be said to have lived outside the cabin than in it. When they did enter, it was like a street door entering a house — swinging in for a moment only to swing back out — with their permanent residence being the open air. Nor did they lose much by this arrangement. In the cabin there was no companionship. Socially, Ahab was unreachable. Though officially counted among Christendom, he was still a stranger to it. He lived in the world as the last of the grizzly bears lived in settled Missouri. And just as when spring and summer have departed, that wild creature buries himself in a hollow tree to live out the winter, sucking his own paws — so in his bitter, howling old age, Ahab's soul, shut up in the cave of his body, fed upon the sullen paws of its gloom!
